title: Consensus Basics
summary: Why distributed nodes need consensus at all, and Raft/Paxos at the depth a design interview expects.

slides.markdown:
Quorums and CRDTs solve conflicts over **data**. But some decisions can't tolerate multiple valid answers at all — who's the leader, which value did a lock actually grant, what's the one true config. **Consensus** is the machinery that gets a group of unreliable nodes to agree on exactly one answer, even if some of them crash or messages get delayed.

This topic covers why that's a genuinely hard problem, what Raft and Paxos guarantee, and where consensus actually shows up versus where a quorum would have been enough.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you need consensus: agreeing on one truth across unreliable nodes
slides.markdown:
**Consensus** is the problem of getting a set of nodes to agree on a single value, even though any node can crash, restart, or fail to receive a message — and the nodes can't tell the difference between "that node is slow" and "that node is dead."

This matters whenever exactly one answer must exist and everyone must agree which one: which node is the leader right now, which client holds a distributed lock, what the current cluster configuration is. Two nodes both believing they're the leader (a **split-brain**) is exactly the failure consensus exists to prevent.

It's a genuinely hard problem — provably impossible to solve with 100% certainty in an asynchronous network with even one faulty node (the FLP result) — which is why production consensus protocols make practical trade-offs rather than chasing perfection.

slides.sectionTitle: What consensus guarantees (and what it costs in latency)
slides.markdown:
A working consensus protocol guarantees two things: **agreement** (every node that decides, decides on the same value) and **validity** (the decided value was actually proposed by someone, not invented). Most practical protocols also need a **majority of nodes** to be alive and reachable to make progress at all — with N nodes, you need at least ⌊N/2⌋+1 to agree.

The cost is coordination: a decision typically requires a round trip to a majority of nodes before it's final, so every consensus-backed operation pays at least one network round trip, sometimes several. This is inherently slower than a single node just deciding on its own — which is exactly the price of the agreement guarantee.

That's why consensus is reserved for decisions that are rare but critical, not the high-volume data path.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a leader election / log replication round at a glance
slides.markdown:
![Three-panel Raft sequence: leader election followed by log replication to a majority](assets/raft-election-and-log.svg)

The two halves of Raft are visible here: **leader election** (a node notices the leader is gone and asks for votes until a majority backs it) and **log replication** (the leader proposes an entry and only commits it once a majority of nodes have durably stored it) — that majority requirement is exactly the same idea as a write quorum.

slides.sectionTitle: Raft at interview depth: leader election + log replication, no more
slides.markdown:
**Raft** breaks consensus into two understandable pieces. **Leader election**: nodes start as followers; if a follower doesn't hear from a leader within a timeout, it becomes a candidate and requests votes; whoever gets a majority becomes leader for a numbered **term**. **Log replication**: once elected, the leader is the only node that accepts new entries, appends them to its log, and replicates them to followers — an entry is only considered committed once a majority of nodes have it durably stored.

That's the interview-depth version: you don't need to reproduce Raft's full state machine, but you should be able to say "a majority elects a leader, and the leader only commits once a majority has replicated the entry" and explain why that majority requirement is what survives a minority of nodes failing.

Raft is the consensus protocol behind etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB's range replication.

slides.sectionTitle: Paxos, briefly: why it's famous and why most systems use Raft instead
slides.markdown:
**Paxos** was the first widely adopted consensus protocol to be proven correct, and it underpins classic systems like Google's Chubby lock service. It solves the same problem as Raft — majority agreement on a single value — through a two-phase proposal process (prepare, then accept) that tolerates nodes failing or messages arriving out of order.

Its reputation problem is notorious: the original paper is famously difficult to map onto a real implementation, and multiple independent teams built subtly different, hard-to-verify variants before understanding it well enough to implement correctly.

Raft was explicitly designed later as "Paxos, but understandable" — same guarantees, but with leader election and log replication made explicit and sequential instead of implicit. That's why almost all new systems reach for Raft, and Paxos shows up mostly in older or academic contexts.

slides.sectionTitle: Where consensus actually shows up: config stores, leader election, distributed locks
slides.markdown:
In practice, you rarely implement Raft or Paxos yourself — you reach for a system that already has it built in. **Config stores** like etcd and ZooKeeper use consensus internally so that every client reads the exact same configuration value, never a stale or conflicting one. **Leader election** for your own service (picking which instance runs a scheduled job, or which shard owner is active) is commonly delegated to one of these stores rather than hand-rolled. **Distributed locks** — "only one worker may process this job" — need consensus underneath, because a lock that two nodes could both believe they hold isn't a lock.

The pattern: build your service to be a *client* of a consensus-backed system, rather than reimplementing consensus for a one-off need.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: consensus-based coordination vs quorum-based storage
slides.markdown:
| | Consensus (Raft/Paxos) | Quorum-based storage (Dynamo-style) |
|---|---|---|
| What it agrees on | One single, strongly ordered value/log | Independent key-value writes, resolved after the fact |
| Conflict handling | Prevented — only one leader proposes at a time | Allowed, then resolved (LWW, vector clocks, CRDTs) |
| Typical use | Leader election, config, distributed locks | High-volume key-value data, shopping carts, sessions |
| Throughput | Lower — every decision needs majority agreement | Higher — writes proceed independently per key |

**How to decide:** use consensus when exactly one answer must exist and disagreement is unacceptable even briefly (who's the leader); use quorum-based storage for high-volume data where a brief, resolvable conflict is an acceptable trade for throughput and availability.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for Paxos/Raft to solve a problem a quorum already solves
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We need strong guarantees on this data, so let's run it through a Raft-backed consensus log."

**Why it's wrong:** consensus is built for agreeing on a single, strictly ordered value or log — it pays a real throughput cost (majority round trips for every decision) to get there. If the actual need is just "most reads should see the latest write" for independent, high-volume key-value data, a tuned quorum (W+R>N) gets you most of that guarantee without funneling every single write through a majority-agreement bottleneck.

**Correct model:** reach for consensus when there must be exactly one authoritative answer and any disagreement (even momentary) is unacceptable — leader election, distributed locks, cluster config. Reach for quorums when you're storing a high volume of independent records and can tolerate resolving occasional conflicts after the fact. Using consensus for the second case burns latency and throughput solving a stronger problem than you actually have.
